# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical Reading of the Varga and Holm Comment on the Halden Pilot

Sections 1 to 5 are a strong, data-based re-analysis. They confirm and put numbers on most of the concerns raised about the Halden paper. Sections 6 to 8 then reach a conclusion that their own data, and the Varden trial they cite, do not support. The corrections show that the Halden gain was **overstated by about half**. They do not show that it was **entirely an artifact**.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures are consistent:

| Item | Check |
|---|---|
| Hours fall, time-tracking organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 → −14.1% ✓ |
| Hours fall, 17-organisation subset | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 → −13.9% ✓ |
| Table 2 gains | 95.1/0.8 → +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 → +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 → +10.8% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 → −2.6% ✓ |

Two figures do not hold up:

- **The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** Section 3 says the remaining four days got 0.7 hours longer, and 1.6 hours a week were worked on the day off. Starting from 32 scheduled hours, that gives 32 + 4 × 0.7 + 1.6 = **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6. Measuring from baseline days of about 8.06 hours gives roughly 36.6. The roughly 2-hour gap could come from leave, holidays or different subsets, but as written the components contradict the total. The headline 34.6 is what Table 2 relies on, so this needs clarifying.
- **The "month ten" extrapolation is off.** Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD over three months, about 0.107 SD a month. Continuing that linearly reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not month ten. Either way, drawing a straight line through two points is weak support for the novelty argument.

## What it does well

- **It uses the underlying microdata.** The comment works from the pilot's own records instead of arguing from the published text.
- **The attrition finding is serious.** If seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, and six cited workload or output, then the Halden description ("withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons") is materially inaccurate. The Halden authors should be asked to respond.
- **It puts numbers on manager bias.** In 19 of 23 organisations the manager's index was higher than the records-based index, by 3.8 points on average.
- **It measures actual hours.** Hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. That is very close to Varden's 13% for case-processing.
- **It settles the revenue question.** The deflation confirms that the reported 1.4% nominal growth was a real-terms fall.
- **It is candid about its subsets.** The data note openly says the corrected figures cover non-random subsets.

## Where it overreaches

### 1. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by evidence the authors cite
The Varden case-processing stratum was randomised, used output from system records, and measured actual hours from timesheets. Those are exactly the three fixes this comment recommends. It still found **+12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9% to +18.4%)**.

That result cannot be explained by self-selection, manager bias or a scheduled-hours denominator. Only novelty remains as an alternative explanation, and novelty has not been shown (point 4 below).

The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature". It also dismisses Varden's meetings analysis. It never mentions Varden's main case-processing result. That is selective use of a single study.

### 2. The two independent estimates agree
After correction, the Halden residual is **+10.8%**. Varden's randomised estimate is **+12.5%**. Two studies with different designs, sectors and biases arrive at a similar per-hour gain of roughly 10 to 12%. That agreement is reasonable evidence that a real effect remains. It is not evidence that the effect is zero.

### 3. The abstract claims more correction than the analysis did
The abstract says the authors "correct the first three" problems, starting with attrition. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described but never quantified. That means:

- The 10.8% is still an estimate among the organisations that stayed in.
- The comment never shows how much of the gain attrition explains.

Both directions are possible. Attrition could lower the figure further. A bounding analysis might also show its effect is modest. The microdata may include month-1 and month-2 output indices for the seven late withdrawals, which would make a bounded intention-to-treat estimate possible.

### 4. Novelty is argued, not tested
The microdata contain **monthly** output indices and time-tracking logs. The direct test of novelty is whether output per actual hour declined from month 1 to month 6. The comment does not report it. Instead it relies on self-reported *energy*, which is not output, extrapolated from two data points.

Saying that six months cannot rule out novelty is fair. Concluding that the remaining effect *is* novelty is not. The honest position is uncertainty, which is not the same as zero. Varden's 24-month follow-up will answer this better than either side's argument.

### 5. Record-based output is not automatically the true figure
Section 2 lists "billable hours delivered" as one of the record-based measures. For organisations using it, output is partly an *hours* measure. It falls mechanically when hours fall, so it will understate any gain per hour. A manager who judges fixed-fee or project output may be measuring something real that billable hours miss.

Manager optimism is plausible, given the 19-of-23 pattern. But the 3.8-point gap is probably part bias and part a mismatch in what is being measured. Splitting the 23 organisations by type of record would show which.

### 6. The meetings critique misdescribes the Varden analysis
- **On selection:** The comment says the offices were "selected for analysis after the results were known". They were all 7 treated case-processing offices, not a chosen subgroup. The calendar data were collected at month six, before the nine-month results. The analysis was unregistered, but that is a different problem.
- **On how Varden framed it:** Varden explicitly said the correlation "cannot establish a mechanism", and it registered a confirmatory test. The comment criticises a stronger claim than the one Varden made.
- **On what the hypothesis implies:** The meetings explanation points to a lasting, non-novelty source of gain, namely removing time that adds little value. If it is confirmed, it undermines the "entirely novelty" conclusion. The right position is to wait for the registered test, not to tell readers never to cite it.

### 7. The conclusion ignores the data note
The data note correctly says the corrected estimates describe the subsets, not the pilot as a whole. The abstract and conclusion then generalise to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. That goes beyond both the pilot and the subsets.

### 8. Smaller points
- **Small groups:** The retail figure of −11.2% rests on three organisations. It is directionally consistent, but it is not a firm estimate.
- **Deflator:** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, and a poor one for non-profit income from grants and donations. The real-terms point still stands, but −2.6% should not be read precisely.
- **Sample size of Varden's counter result:** Calling it the "most reliable finding" fits its design, but it rests on 5 offices against 5 and has the widest confidence intervals in that trial.

## Where the three documents leave things

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Was the Halden 23.4% overstated? | **Yes, by about half.** Manager bias, the scheduled-hours denominator and non-random attrition all contributed. |
| Is there a real gain in output per actual hour in work that can be queued? | **Probably, about 10–12%.** The randomised Varden result and the corrected Halden subset agree. |
| Is that gain durable? | **Unknown.** Novelty is possible but untested. Monthly Halden data and the Varden 24-month follow-up are the ways to test it. |
| Does it work where output depends on staff presence? | **No, at least without extra staff.** Output fell by roughly 7–11% and service got worse, in both datasets. |
| What explains any gain? | **Open.** Fewer meetings is a plausible, testable hypothesis. Rest is asserted but not measured. |

The comment's recommendations are sound: record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up, and intention-to-treat analysis. Its own conclusion should have stayed as cautious as its data note.
